Blue-Green Algae: Troubled Waters

By: Bernadette Maguire | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A looming water crisis is going to make Eskom and Acid mine drainage pale by comparison.

Summary:
The issue of Blue Greens has not received public attention as it should. These organisms are primitive, being neither plant nor animal but both. They are amongst the first living organisms that evolved on Earth, originally into a hostile environment where there was no oxygen and severe radiation from the sun because of the absence of an atmosphere. They are extremely resilient and are an indicator of severely distressed aquatic ecosystems. They produced our first oxygen and also evolved a number of complex molecules to protect themselves including sun block. They also produce a toxin known as microcystin, which they eject when in distress.

Now here’s the issue – we have the highest known levels of contamination in the world. The Americans get concerned at 20 microgrammes per litre, but we have 10,000 spiking at 18,000 and nobody is concerned. We now know that about 2/3 o our national resource is contaminated from the attached paper. We also know that the toxin is released when the organism gets stressed. We know that blue-greens are found in large dams like Vaal and Midmar. We also know that the current bulk water treatment processes do not eliminate microcystin toxin once released. The only known treatment is with activated carbon and at present this is only available as an end-of-pipe solution, not yet as a bulk treatment solution.




Further information:
There is also a linkage with death of crocodiles by means of pansteatitis. This occurs when the fatty tissue in the animal is rejected by the confused auto immune system, first bloating and then killing the beast. This means that ancient creatures that survived the dinosaur mass extinction are no match to human-induced plagues arising from dysfunctional sewage works. We could reference this in Kruger in 2009.

It also means that unless we get our sewage management sorted out in SA, we are on the very brink of a catastrophe that makes Eskom pale into insignificance. Not wanting to be alarmist, but this is the reality of the problem we are facing.

Mark Matthews from UCT has published a scientific paper on this important issue using satellite images over a 10 year period to show the extent of the problem. I'd like to do testing with Dr Anthony Turton to corroborate this and then also plan to use one municipality as a case study. One of the muncipalities adjacent to a big water source might be suitable.

Press Release:


South Africa is in the grip of the worst ever El Nino event in recorded history. But experts say the problem of dwindling water supply pales in comparison to the problem of water quality. Blue-green algae - an organism that releases a toxin similar to snake venom - has infiltrated two thirds of South Africa's drinking-water sources. Removing it is an extensive and expensive process, raising fears that South Africa could soon be facing a serious drinking water crisis. Carte Blanche asks - is our tap water safe to drink?

Script:


Troubled Waters

VO: 19”

South Africa is caught in the grip of what scientists describe as the most extreme and protracted El nino event in recorded history. To date 4 provinces have been declared drought disaster areas. Extreme conditions in Kwazulu natal have seen the levels in Hazelmere dam slipping to a perilous 25%. And Gauteng residents are facing phase two water restrictions. But dwindling reserves aren’t the biggest issue says water expert Dr Anthony Turton.

Anthony:
Water quality is our big challenge not water quantity. While water quantity is a serious matter in its own right, the water quality its silent thing that comes through.

VO: 8”
What worries him most is this – cyanobacteria or what’s commonly known as blue green algae. Organisms that are 3 and a half billion years old.

Anthony:
So your cyanobacteria are the first single celled life forms that are known to exist and because they are single celled and because they are the oldest they are neither plant nor animal. So they are neither plant no animal so they are very primitive.

John link:
It’s estimated that between 50 and 70% of our water resevoirs are contaminated. Now according to some experts those contamination levels are the highest in the world.

VO: 19
Previously government estimates suggested that around 5% of our dams were affected but new remote sensing technology using satellite images over a 10 year period show that the concentrations are in fact far higher. This pioneering work was done by Dr Mark Matthews and funded by the CSIR.

Mark:
The problem is severe and widespread. In all of those dams we had cyanobacteria occurring at one stage or another and in more than 26 of the dams we had frequent cyanobacteria bloom occurences.

VO: 7
The Vaal dam, that supplies drinking water to roughly 12 million people in Gauteng, looks bleak in this satellite image.

Mark:
We can see large areas of the lake is covered with cyanobacteria which is represented by the bright green colour on the screen.

VO: 17”
The problem with blue green algae is that it releases a toxin called microsystin when the cell breaks open during water treatment – a toxin that’s been compared to snake venom.
But getting rid of the blue green algae is well at best complicated.

Anthony:
If you bring them out of a dam, suck them out of a dam into your pump, and you now put them through a filtration system and part of that process involves anything that is stressful for example chlorine, they suddenly detect the stress and their final message to you is, I am stressed thank you heres the gift that keeps on giving. That’s the problem.

VO: 4”
So removing the toxins means additional treatment with chlorine or activated carbon – increasing treatment costs.

Mark:
They produce these geosmin compounds that lead to complaints with regard tto the taste , this earthy taste.

John link
The cyanobacteria are more than just a threat to our dwindling water resources, They also come with a variety of health hazards some of them can be fatal.

VO:
Researchers have linked the toxin to cancer, alzheimers and motor neuron disease - the disease that struck down rugby player Joost van der Westhuizen. Dr Rachael Dunlop’s an Australian scientist was the lead researcher on a groundbreaking paper on MND. Her search for answers took her to the Pacific island of Guam which has the highest concentration of Motor neuron disease in the world. She discovered out that cyanobacteria was present of the roots of cycads and the seeds were used to make tortillas, a favourite food.

Rachael:
So they were getting a dose of the toxin through the flour in addition they had a voracious appetite for fruit bats so fruit bats were feeding on the seeds of this particular tree so the locals were getting a dose of the toxin when they ate the fruitbats.

John:
What is it specifically about this toxin that leads to such a devastating disease.

Rachael”
If it’s in our bodies when we are making proteins it gets stuck in our proteins by mistake and this can lead to those proteins becoming toxic, building up and causing those cells to die and we think this may be a trigger for motor neuron disease in susceptible people.

VO
We need more research but another hypothesis is that the toxins may be present in the fertilizer used on sports fields and that this may be how Joost and others ingested the toxin. In places like Zeekoevlei on the Cape falts there have been also been cases of animals dying as a result of drinking toxic dam water..

Mark:
There have been a number of recorded deaths of animals and things like that, even at this lake here there was a case of someone’s dog dying as a result of cyanobacteria poisoning.

VO: 5”
Hartebeespoort dam in the north west province is not only choked up with hyacinths its also awash with cyanobacteria blooms.

Mark:
Hartebeespoort dam for sure is almost like a chemical for cyanobacteria blooms. Its got very high concentrations of nutrients coming into it, its an extremely warm climate so it’s a kind of freak in terms of production, its one of the most productive resevoirs in the world actually.

VO:8”
Hartebeespoort resident and founding member of their water action group, Rick van Rossum is all too familiar with the algae.

Rick:
Blue green algae when it decomposes becomes a terrible product,very difficult to live with, it smells so bad that most people imagine it to be sewage and its not sewage at all. It impacts on property values, it impacts on your lifestyle and its just a mess to have.


VO: 7”
Dysfunctional sewerage systems are the main reason our dams are so polluted and it’s the reason cyanobacteria flourish,

Mark:
You can imagine throwing a bag of fertilizer into your swimming pool, you wouldn’t be surprised if the next day you came back and it was bright green.

Rick:
Everything north of the Hillbrow ridge flows into the hartebeespoort dam and that’s millions of people and their sewage and their effluents is treated by the sewage plants but they can’t always cope and we have a lot of informal settlements who don’t have the privilege of running their effluent through a sewage works so is directly into the rivers.

VO: 6”
Dr Turton estimates the problem is 200 times greater than acid mine drainage contamination. That’s because only 20% of our sewerage works are operating optimally.

Anthony:
Which leaves the remaining 80% which for rounded up purposes is 4000 mega litres of sewage untreated or at best partially treated per day going into our rivers and dams.

VO: 16”
Couple this with the drought and we’re facing a double calamity because with no rain the sewerage isn’t being diluted leaving the water bodies distressed. Department of Water Affairs spokesman Sputnik Ratau admits that it’s a problem.

Sputnik:
It is a serious issue where you have the waste water treatment works that do not function optimally they also create a very good arena or situation for the cyanobacteria to thrive.

VO: 17”
Given the parlous state of some of our municipalities like Madibeng near Hartebeespoort his department had to side step the local authorities and step in. They’ve also had to throw millions of rands at Hartebeespoort and have set up a monioring unit to manage the high levels of toxins.

Sputnik:
Harties will continue for a while to be a bit of a setback for us because of the influence of some of the effluent that comes from other areas. We will make sure that at some point we can able to say that we are now at the right quality of the water in there.

John:
But we are not there yet though?

Sputnik:
No not there yet.

VO: 11”
Then throw into the mix the fact that we are the most medicated humans on the planet ever and these partially metabolized medications are making it into our water resevoirs too.

Anthony:
Now we have got these chemicals and drugs and partially treated sewage going into this biological reactor, Hartebeespoort dam, Midmar dam call it whatever you want to. Under stressful conditions, elevated temperatures, elevated amounts of nutrient flows. Well what’s now going to happen? Well things speciate, chemicals speciate, bacteria mutate, viruses mutate.

John:
What you’ve just described is quite terrifying. Effectively our dams are toxic soups?

Anthony.
Primordial toxic soups!

VO: 5”
Which may explain why the agricultural sector around Harties is being shunned.

Rick van Rossum:
There are several large retailers in this country that have stopped purchasing their products from down river of the Hartebeespoort because of the possible pollution problems that they get. Its scared away or rather killed the tobacco industry down the river. We used to have a very big tobacco industry all the way down to the Limpopo. It’s completely gone.

VO: 16”
This week it emerged in the press that despite this looming catastrophe the Department of Water Affairs and sanitation underspent by 2 billion in the past financial year 700 million of that meant for the Madibeng area which has been plagued by dysfunctional water and sewerage systems.

John:
On the ground what are the implications of that underspending?


Sputnik:
In relation to where water treatment works or water treatment plants were not working optimally there would be an impact on the quality of water supply.

John:
We’ve spoken to a number of experts who say we are sitting on a ticking time bomb. That the signs really aren’t good. Are they over reacting?

Sputnik:
I think as I indicated earlier the issue of cyanobacteria is a concern for us. The fact that we don’t have sufficient water right now to naturally dilute bacteria that is in our rivers and so on the makes the whole thing worse.

VO:
For now the department assures us our drinking water meets international standards but Dr Turton isn’t convinced given the high mycosistin concentrations.

Anthony:
If that blue green gets into the bulk water supply, the most sophisticated plant in the country is unable to deal with it. So that now raises another question, if you are a scientist with a social conscience as I happen to be, okay. What do you do? Do you just keep quiet and participate unwittingly in this experiment or do you actually speak out.

John Link
What we need now is a concerted effort by national and local authorities to mitigate the cyanobacteria and to do whatever they can to protect our precious water resource.

VO:
Dr Matthews would like to see additional filtering of river water using retaining wetlands before it flows into our reservoirs. He’s also set up an online monitoring service for over a hundred dams around the country.

Mark:
We’re also building a website where the public can go and access information on their dam in their real time from 2016 onwards taking advantage of satellites which have been launched in the last couple of years.

VO:
Dr Turton believes that what we need more than anything is more research. We need to nurture and liberate our scientists to unpack the unknowns.

Anthony:
Really it’s a no brainer – all of the evidence that is coming back, is overwhelming. It’s absolutely overwhelming. When you don’t know what it is that you don’t know, that’s your biggest risk. When you start to know what it is that you don’t know, now you’re dealing with the problem.

Promos (1):

VO: 7”
Is our drinking water facing a double calamity as the drought coupled with undiluted pollutants turn our resevoirs into primordial toxic soups.

Anthony:…Midmar dam


Promo (2)

VO: 9”
Ground breaking remote sensing satellite images show that our dams have have the high est concentrations of blue green algae in the world.

Anthony:
If the blue green…sophisticated plant unable to deal with it.


Promo (3):

VO: 10”
Experts describe it as a threat 200 times greater than acid mine drainage – why the silence on blue green algae in our water caused by our dysfunctional sewerage systems?

Rick: Everything north of the Hillbrow ridge flows into the hartebeespoort dam and that’s millions of people and their sewage and their effluents is treated by the sewage plants but they can’t always cope and we have a lot of informal settlements who don’t have the privilege of running their effluent through a sewage works so is directly into the rivers. VO: 6” Dr Turton estimates the problem is 200 times greater than acid mine drainage contamination. That’s because only 20% of our sewerage works are operating optimally. Anthony: Which leaves the remaining 80% which for rounded up purposes is 4000 mega litres of sewage untreated or at best partially treated per day going into our rivers and dams. VO: 16” Couple this with the drought and we’re facing a double calamity because with no rain the sewerage isn’t being diluted leaving the water bodies distressed. Department of Water Affairs spokesman Sputnik Ratau admits that it’s a problem. Sputnik: It is a serious issue where you have the waste water treatment works that do not function optimally they also create a very good arena or situation for the cyanobacteria to thrive. VO: 17” Given the parlous state of some of our municipalities like Madibeng near Hartebeespoort his department had to side step the local authorities and step in. They’ve also had to throw millions of rands at Hartebeespoort and have set up a monioring unit to manage the high levels of toxins. Sputnik: Harties will continue for a while to be a bit of a setback for us because of the influence of some of the effluent that comes from other areas. We will make sure that at some point we can able to say that we are now at the right quality of the water in there. John: But we are not there yet though? Sputnik: No not there yet. VO: 11” Then throw into the mix the fact that we are the most medicated humans on the planet ever and these partially metabolized medications are making it into our water resevoirs too. Anthony: Now we have got these chemicals and drugs and partially treated sewage going into this biological reactor, Hartebeespoort dam, Midmar dam call it whatever you want to. Under stressful conditions, elevated temperatures, elevated amounts of nutrient flows. Well what’s now going to happen? Well things speciate, chemicals speciate, bacteria mutate, viruses mutate. John: What you’ve just described is quite terrifying. Effectively our dams are toxic soups? Anthony. Primordial toxic soups! VO: 5” Which may explain why the agricultural sector around Harties is being shunned. Rick van Rossum: There are several large retailers in this country that have stopped purchasing their products from down river of the Hartebeespoort because of the possible pollution problems that they get. Its scared away or rather killed the tobacco industry down the river. We used to have a very big tobacco industry all the way down to the Limpopo. It’s completely gone. VO: 16” This week it emerged in the press that despite this looming catastrophe the Department of Water Affairs and sanitation underspent by 2 billion in the past financial year 700 million of that meant for the Madibeng area which has been plagued by dysfunctional water and sewerage systems. John: On the ground what are the implications of that underspending? Sputnik: In relation to where water treatment works or water treatment plants were not working optimally there would be an impact on the quality of water supply. John: We’ve spoken to a number of experts who say we are sitting on a ticking time bomb. That the signs really aren’t good. Are they over reacting? Sputnik: I think as I indicated earlier the issue of cyanobacteria is a concern for us. The fact that we don’t have sufficient water right now to naturally dilute bacteria that is in our rivers and so on the makes the whole thing worse. VO: For now the department assures us our drinking water meets international standards but Dr Turton isn’t convinced given the high mycosistin concentrations. Anthony: If that blue green gets into the bulk water supply, the most sophisticated plant in the country is unable to deal with it. So that now raises another question, if you are a scientist with a social conscience as I happen to be, okay. What do you do? Do you just keep quiet and participate unwittingly in this experiment or do you actually speak out. John Link What we need now is a concerted effort by national and local authorities to mitigate the cyanobacteria and to do whatever they can to protect our precious water resource. VO: Dr Matthews would like to see additional filtering of river water using retaining wetlands before it flows into our reservoirs. He’s also set up an online monitoring service for over a hundred dams around the country. Mark: We’re also building a website where the public can go and access information on their dam in their real time from 2016 onwards taking advantage of satellites which have been launched in the last couple of years. VO: Dr Turton believes that what we need more than anything is more research. We need to nurture and liberate our scientists to unpack the unknowns. Anthony: Really it’s a no brainer – all of the evidence that is coming back, is overwhelming. It’s absolutely overwhelming. When you don’t know what it is that you don’t know, that’s your biggest risk. When you start to know what it is that you don’t know, now you’re dealing with the problem. Promos (1): VO: 7” Is our drinking water facing a double calamity as the drought coupled with undiluted pollutants turn our resevoirs into primordial toxic soups. Anthony:…Midmar dam Promo (2) VO: 9” Ground breaking remote sensing satellite images show that our dams have have the high est concentrations of blue green algae in the world. Anthony: If the blue green…sophisticated plant unable to deal with it. Promo (3): VO: 10” Experts describe it as a threat 200 times greater than acid mine drainage – why the silence on blue green algae in our water caused by our dysfunctional sewerage systems?

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): A looming water crisis is going to make Eskom and Acid mine drainage pale by comparison.
metadata.Summary: The issue of Blue Greens has not received public attention as it should. These organisms are primitive, being neither plant nor animal but both. They are amongst the first living organisms that evolved on Earth, originally into a hostile environment where there was no oxygen and severe radiation from the sun because of the absence of an atmosphere. They are extremely resilient and are an indicator of severely distressed aquatic ecosystems. They produced our first oxygen and also evolved a number of complex molecules to protect themselves including sun block. They also produce a toxin known as microcystin, which they eject when in distress. Now here’s the issue – we have the highest known levels of contamination in the world. The Americans get concerned at 20 microgrammes per litre, but we have 10,000 spiking at 18,000 and nobody is concerned. We now know that about 2/3 o our national resource is contaminated from the attached paper. We also know that the toxin is released when the organism gets stressed. We know that blue-greens are found in large dams like Vaal and Midmar. We also know that the current bulk water treatment processes do not eliminate microcystin toxin once released. The only known treatment is with activated carbon and at present this is only available as an end-of-pipe solution, not yet as a bulk treatment solution.
metadata.Further information: There is also a linkage with death of crocodiles by means of pansteatitis. This occurs when the fatty tissue in the animal is rejected by the confused auto immune system, first bloating and then killing the beast. This means that ancient creatures that survived the dinosaur mass extinction are no match to human-induced plagues arising from dysfunctional sewage works. We could reference this in Kruger in 2009. It also means that unless we get our sewage management sorted out in SA, we are on the very brink of a catastrophe that makes Eskom pale into insignificance. Not wanting to be alarmist, but this is the reality of the problem we are facing. Mark Matthews from UCT has published a scientific paper on this important issue using satellite images over a 10 year period to show the extent of the problem. I'd like to do testing with Dr Anthony Turton to corroborate this and then also plan to use one municipality as a case study. One of the muncipalities adjacent to a big water source might be suitable. Other interviews: Dr Anthony turton Dr Mark Matthews
